function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
I’m unable to run `git clone`, `git add`, `git commit` or `git push` from here, but I can give you everything you need to put into the repository and the exact shell commands you’ll run locally.  
Below is a complete set‑up for the **nodejs‑welcome** repo:

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repo (run locally)

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse & Create Files

### 2.1 Dockerfile

Create a file named `Dockerfile` at the repo root with the following content:

```dockerfile
# Use the official lightweight Node.js image
FROM node:18-alpine

# Set working directory inside the container
WORKDIR /app

# Copy package files first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install production dependencies only
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the application code
COPY . .

# Expose the port your app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Default command to start the app
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * `node:18-alpine` is small, fast, and contains the Node runtime needed for the repo.  
> * `npm ci` guarantees a clean install of the exact versions in `package-lock.json`.  
> * The container listens on port **3000**, which matches the default port used by the sample app.

---

### 2.2 Kubernetes YAML

Create a directory called `k8s` (or `deployments`) and inside it create a file named `deployment.yaml` with the following content:

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: <YOUR_REGISTRY>/nodejs-welcome:latest   # replace with your registry
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer          # change to NodePort/ClusterIP if you prefer
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80                  # external port
    targetPort: 3000          # container port
```

> **What to replace?**  
> * `<YOUR_REGISTRY>` – e.g., `ghcr.io/zelarhq` or `docker.io/zelarhq`.  
> * If you’re deploying to a cluster that doesn’t support `LoadBalancer`, switch to `NodePort` or `ClusterIP`.

---

### 2.3 GitHub Actions Workflow

Create a folder `.github/workflows` (if it doesn’t exist) and add a file named `ci.yml`:

```yaml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build-and-deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      # Checkout the repo
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3

      # Set up Docker Buildx (multi‑arch support)
      - name: Set up Docker Buildx
        uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v2

      # Log in to Docker Hub (or your registry)
      - name: Log in to Docker Hub
        uses: docker/login-action@v2
        with:
          username: ${{ secrets.DOCKER_USERNAME }}
          password: ${{ secrets.DOCKER_PASSWORD }}

      # Build and push the Docker image
      - name: Build and push Docker image
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
        with:
          context: .
          push: true
          tags: ${{ secrets.DOCKER_USERNAME }}/nodejs-welcome:latest

      # Deploy to Kubernetes (requires a kubeconfig secret)
      - name: Deploy to Kubernetes
        uses: azure/k8s-deploy@v3
        with:
          manifests: |
            ./k8s/deployment.yaml
          images: ${{ secrets.DOCKER_USERNAME }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
          kubeconfig: ${{ secrets.KUBECONFIG }}   # optional if you want to deploy automatically
```

> **Secrets you’ll need to add in the repo settings → Secrets → Actions**  
> * `DOCKER_USERNAME` – your Docker Hub (or other registry) username.  
> * `DOCKER_PASSWORD` – your Docker Hub password or personal access token.  
> * `KUBECONFIG` – optional; if you want the workflow to apply the manifest directly to a cluster.

---

## 3️⃣ Add All Changed Files

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & Push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes YAML, and GitHub Actions CI pipeline"
git push origin main
```

---

### Quick Checklist

| Step | Command | Notes |
|------|---------|-------|
| Clone | `git clone ...` | Done locally |
| Create Dockerfile | `touch Dockerfile && echo ... > Dockerfile` | Or use a text editor |
| Create Kubernetes YAML | `mkdir -p k8s && touch k8s/deployment.yaml && echo ... > k8s/deployment.yaml` | |
| Create GitHub Actions | `mkdir -p .github/workflows && touch .github/workflows/ci.yml && echo ... > .github/workflows/ci.yml` | |
| Add | `git add ...` | |
| Commit | `git commit -m "..."` | |
| Push | `git push origin main` | |

Once pushed, the workflow will trigger on every push to `main`, build the Docker image, push it to your registry, and (optionally) apply the Kubernetes manifest.

Feel free to tweak the image tag, number of replicas, or service type to match your environment. Happy coding!
